title: Disney’s new Star Wars animatronics use AWS AI to react to guests
excerpt: ‘The first time we will personalize that experience’: Disney’s Star Wars animatronics react to guests with AWS AI.
content_html:
Disney has built three Star Wars animatronics that react to guests and to each other with no one controlling them. Amazon Web Services supplies the AI. Walt Disney Imagineering named the three Anzellans Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a and Jibu Bre’a in a post on Wednesday.

Disney’s Audio-Animatronics have run on fixed, scripted loops since the Enchanted Tiki Room opened at Disneyland in 1963. The Anzellans instead notice what is happening around them, Disney said. They decide for themselves what to say and how to move.

“When we launch with the Anzellans at re:Invent, it’ll be really the first time in which we will personalize that experience based on who that guest is,” Kyle Laughlin, who leads Imagineering R&D, told The Hollywood Reporter.

Guests can meet them first at Amazon’s re:Invent conference in Las Vegas, from 30 November to 4 December. Disney has not said when they will reach its parks.

AI picks the line, Imagineers write it

Each character has cameras and microphones. They can tell how many people stand in front of them and their rough ages. They also spot a birthday button or a Star Wars T-shirt, Laughlin told CNET.

The AI does not write their dialogue. Imagineers recorded hundreds of thousands of lines in a mix of English and Anzellan, according to CNET. The system chooses which to play. The characters have set personalities: Vilo is the boss, Kado the attention-seeking mechanic, and Jibu, Kado’s twin, the shy one.

The system runs on Amazon Bedrock, which lets Imagineers switch between AI models from different companies. AWS staff used Kiro, Amazon’s AI coding agent, to turn Imagineering’s creative briefs into software, which humans then reviewed. The project took “mere months”, Laughlin said.

“These Anzellans now are our most advanced Audio-Animatronics in the world,” Laughlin told TechRadar.

What happens to the camera data

Disney uses the data from an encounter only for that moment, Laughlin told TechRadar. It does not keep the data in the cloud to reuse, and it does not train AI models on it. If the system fails, the characters fall back to another experience.

The Anzellans run on the same robotic platform as Disney’s free-roaming Olaf and its BDX droids, according to TechRadar. Laughlin said guests will meet them indoors first, in shops.

Disney’s cost cuts

The launch comes a day after Disney said it is targeting $3bn in yearly savings by 2029, CNBC reported. Finance chief Hugh Johnston told CNBC: “We do expect more layoffs.” Disney had already planned thousands of layoffs.

At the same time, Disney is spending on technology. It hired its first chief technology officer from Character.AI and agreed to pay for Character.AI staff. Earlier this month it signed an AI alliance with Adobe.
